faqs.question: Do most Canadians actually take part in Halloween?
faqs.answer: About two-thirds do something: children trick-or-treat door to door on the evening of 31 October, houses are decorated and pumpkins carved. An October 2025 Narrative Research poll found half of Canadian adults hand out treats, a third decorate outside and a quarter wear a costume.

faqs.question: Where were Halloween house visits first recorded in Canada?
faqs.answer: In Vancouver. The Dictionary of Canadianisms quotes an 1898 Vancouver Daily World item describing young people paying friendly visits to houses in disguise on Halloween night, three decades before the phrase 'trick or treat' appeared in print.

faqs.question: Is Halloween a statutory holiday in Canada?
faqs.answer: No. Halloween is not a statutory or public holiday in any province or territory, so schools and workplaces stay open when it falls on a weekday. In 2026 and 2027 it falls on a Saturday and a Sunday.

faqs.question: When is Halloween in Canada in 2026 and 2027?
faqs.answer: Halloween is always 31 October: Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027. In both years it is still on daylight saving time, because the clocks fall back on the following Sunday, 1 November 2026 and 7 November 2027.

faqs.question: Was "trick or treat" first said in Canada?
faqs.answer: It was first printed there. The Dictionary of Canadianisms records 'tricks or treats' and 'treat or trick' in Ontario in 1917, and the exact phrase 'trick or treat' in a November 1927 report from Blackie, Alberta, printed in The Lethbridge Herald.

faqs.question: Is it usually snowing on Halloween in Canada?
faqs.answer: In the North and parts of the Prairies, often. Environment Canada's 1981–2010 normals give Yellowknife 20.9 cm of October snow and Edmonton 10.4 cm, while Vancouver and Halifax get rain instead, more than 120 mm in the month.

faqs.question: How do kids trick-or-treat in the cold?
faqs.answer: Many wear the costume over a snowsuit, so costumes are bought a size up and face paint replaces masks that fog. Keep reflective strips visible on the outer layer and loose fabric away from candle-lit pumpkins.

faqs.question: What do people in Quebec call Halloween?
faqs.answer: Quebec French uses the article: 'C'est l'Halloween!', with Halloween treated as a feminine noun, so the greeting is 'Joyeuse Halloween'. Quebec also hands out fewer treats: 34% of adults in the 2025 poll, against 58% in the Prairies and Atlantic Canada.

faqs.question: Do the clocks change around Halloween in Canada?
faqs.answer: Yes, right after. Daylight saving time ends at 2:00 a.m. on Sunday 1 November 2026 and Sunday 7 November 2027, except in most of Saskatchewan and in Yukon, which keep the same time all year.

faqs.question: How much do Canadians spend on Halloween?
faqs.answer: We could not find a dated Canadian spending figure we could verify: the Retail Council of Canada site returned an access error. Treat any US spending number you see as American, not Canadian.

# Halloween in Canada: Snowsuits, Prairie Firsts and l'Halloween

Halloween in Canada is celebrated on 31 October with door-to-door trick-or-treating, costumes and carved pumpkins, but it is not a statutory holiday in any province or territory. It lands on a Saturday in 2026 and a Sunday in 2027. Canada also has a solid claim on the phrase itself: the earliest known printed "trick or treat" is a November 1927 report from Blackie, Alberta. About half of Canadian adults hand out treats, according to an October 2025 survey of 1,230 people.

Sending a Halloween greeting to someone in Canada instead? SubhSandesh figures: phones account for 48.3% of opens of shared pages, and a page averages 11.1 views, measured across every template, not Halloween alone.

Below: who celebrates, why, the 1927 claim checked, October weather by city, a regional table and the clock change.

## How do Canadians celebrate Halloween?

Mostly at the front door. A [Narrative Research and Logit Group poll published 29 October 2025](https://narrativeresearch.ca/canadas-halloween-habits-unmasked-half-give-treats-one-third-decorate-and-one-quarter-dress-up/) found that half of Canadian adults give out treats, one-third decorate the outside of their home, a quarter decorate inside and a quarter put on a costume themselves.

The regional split is the striking part. In the Prairies and Atlantic Canada, 58% hand out treats; in Quebec the figure is 34%. Younger and higher-income Canadians were the most likely to take part. The poll ran online from 7 to 9 October 2025 and was weighted to the 2021 Census by gender, age and region.

Of the decorators, 40% reuse last year's props, about half add something new each season, and one in ten buy fresh decorations every year.

On spending, we have nothing solid to give you. We could not reach a Retail Council of Canada Halloween release (its site returned an access error) and found no other dated Canadian spending survey, so this page prints no Canadian spending figure rather than borrow an American one.

## Why is Halloween celebrated in Canada?

Because nineteenth-century Canada adopted it on purpose. Historian Adrien Lherm argues in a peer-reviewed 2005 article in *Communications*, [*Halloween, une vieille fête britannique dans la modernité américaine*](https://www.persee.fr/doc/comm_0588-8018_2005_num_77_1_2264), that while Halloween was fading from the British calendar it grew into a popular event in Canada and the United States.

His explanation is pointed. According to the article's abstract, North Americans took the festival up precisely for its old British associations, as a way to keep Canada and the US culturally Anglo-Saxon during waves of new immigration, then adapted its rites to fast-changing industrial life. We read only the abstract, so we cite nothing beyond it.

The door-to-door part arrived early on the west coast. The *Dictionary of Canadianisms on Historical Principles* (DCHP-3) records an 1898 *Vancouver Daily World* item describing young people paying friendly visits to houses in disguise on Halloween night, decades before anyone had a name for it.

## Did Canada really coin "trick or treat"?

Yes, with a footnote most retellings skip. The [DCHP-3 entry for "trick or treat"](https://dchp.arts.ubc.ca/entries/trick%20or%20treat), revised April 2025 at the University of British Columbia, labels the chant a Canadianism of origin, and its evidence starts in Ontario, not Alberta.

### The Ontario variants, 1917

The *Sault Star* of 1917 reported gangs calling out "tricks or treats", with both nouns plural. The same year, the Owen Sound *Sun* recorded children greeting a householder with "treat or trick", the words reversed. A 1924 *Edmonton Bulletin* item calls "Treat up -- or tricks" the familiar Hallowe'en ultimatum.

### The Alberta wording, 1927

The modern word order first turns up in a report datelined Blackie, Alberta, 3 November 1927, printed in *The Lethbridge Herald* under the headline "TRICK OR TREAT" IS DEMAND. Blackie is the town; Lethbridge is the paper. Word historian Barry Popik reports that the same Blackie item ran in the *Calgary Daily Herald* a day earlier, on 3 November; we could not open that page ourselves.

DCHP-3 also quotes Canadians in 1989 and 2002 remembering the cry "Halloween apples" used in place of "trick or treat", a reminder that the chant was never uniform.

So the fair summary is this: the chant's family began in Ontario in 1917, and its current wording is first attested from rural Alberta in 1927. Neither is proof of who said it first aloud, only of who printed it.

## What is the weather like on Halloween in Canada?

It depends enormously on the province. Environment and Climate Change Canada's [1981–2010 Canadian Climate Normals](https://climate.weather.gc.ca/climate_normals/index_e.html) for October, at each city's main airport station, show the spread:

- **Yellowknife:** mean daily high 0.9°C, low −4.2°C, 20.9 cm of October snow and about 6 cm on the ground by month's end.
- **Edmonton:** high 10.4°C, low −2.9°C, 10.4 cm of October snow.
- **Winnipeg:** high 10.5°C, low −0.5°C, 4.8 cm of snow.
- **Vancouver:** high 13.5°C, low 7.0°C, 120.8 mm of precipitation and almost no snow.
- **Halifax:** high 13.1°C, low 4.2°C, 124.9 mm of precipitation.

These are monthly averages, so 31 October itself usually runs a little colder than the October mean, and trick-or-treating happens after dark, nearer the overnight low. In practice that means rain gear on the coasts and real winter clothing north of the 60th parallel.

### Costumes over snowsuits

On the Prairies and in the North, children often wear the costume over a snowsuit, so buy or sew it one size up and skip anything tight at the shoulders. Masks fog in the cold, which is a good reason to choose face paint instead.

Fabric matters too. Health Canada's [recall of a polyester Halloween witch hat](https://recalls-rappels.canada.ca/en/alert-recall/claire-s-and-icing-stores-halloween-witch-hat-recalled-due-flammability-hazard) (last updated 11 July 2024) says the hat failed recognized flammability standards and posed a burn risk, although no injuries had been reported. Keep capes and trailing hems away from pumpkin candles.

## Halloween across Canada's regions

The country is too large for one Halloween. The table compares regions using the poll and climate figures above.

| Region | Notable custom | Late-October weather (ECCC normal) | Language note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quebec | Lowest treat-giving: 34% hand out treats | Montreal high 13.0°C, 1.8 cm October snow | French: *l'Halloween*, feminine |
| Atlantic Canada | Highest treat-giving: 58% | Halifax 124.9 mm, St. John's 156.2 mm rain and snow | English; Acadian French in parts of NB and NS |
| Prairies and North | "Trick or treat" first printed, 1927 | Edmonton 10.4 cm snow, Yellowknife 20.9 cm | "Treat up -- or tricks" in Edmonton, 1924 |
| British Columbia | Disguised house visits recorded in 1898 | Vancouver 120.8 mm, near-zero snow | Period spelling "Hallowe'en" |

The takeaway: weather and language change more across Canada than the ritual does.

### Quebec: l'Halloween

Quebec French puts an article in front of the name. The Office québécois de la langue française treats *Halloween* as a feminine noun with a silent *h*, so a Quebecer says *C'est l'Halloween!* where speakers in France would usually drop the article. The greeting is *Joyeuse Halloween*.

### Atlantic Canada

Atlantic doorsteps are the most generous in the 2025 poll, tied with the Prairies at 58%. They are also the wettest: St. John's averages 156.2 mm of October precipitation, the highest of the cities above, so umbrellas and waterproof boots are part of many costumes.

### The Prairies and the North

The Prairies hold both the 1924 Edmonton ultimatum and the 1927 Blackie report, which makes the region the cradle of the modern wording. With Edmonton's October low at −2.9°C and Yellowknife's high barely above freezing, the snowsuit question settles itself.

## Halloween 2026 and 2027: dates, holidays and the clock change

Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027, so in both years it lands on a weekend. It is not a statutory or public holiday anywhere in Canada; the Canada Revenue Agency's 2026 list of public holidays has nothing between Thanksgiving (Monday 12 October) and Remembrance Day (Wednesday 11 November).

Clocks change right after. The [National Research Council Canada](https://nrc.canada.ca/en/certifications-evaluations-standards/canadas-official-time/time-zones-daylight-saving-time) says daylight saving time ends at 2:00 a.m. local time on the first Sunday of November, which makes it Sunday 1 November 2026 and Sunday 7 November 2027.

Two exceptions matter. Most of Saskatchewan stays on Central Standard Time all year, with only the Lloydminster area changing clocks as Alberta does, and Yukon has used UTC−7 year-round since 2020. Everywhere else, Halloween evening is still on daylight time, so dusk arrives about an hour later on the clock than it will once the clocks fall back.

## Sending a Halloween greeting to someone in Canada

If the person you want to surprise lives in Calgary or Halifax while you are elsewhere, a link travels faster than a parcel. The [interactive Halloween card](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) suits exactly one recipient. Their visit runs through a small haunted house: three knocks at the door, sweets falling to catch, a pumpkin to carve until the word you picked lights up, foggy portraits hiding as many as six of your photos, and your letter read under a flashlight beam.

The closing question defaults to "Will you be my boo?" and takes up to 60 characters of your own wording; afterwards they can save a Boo License sized 1080×1920 for Stories. Pick partner, bestie, family or kids mode; the kids version keeps ghosts round and blushing with nothing gory or sudden. Their first answer reaches you as an email.

One honest limit for this audience: the interface is in English. A Quebec grandparent who reads no English will get more from a handwritten French card, though you can still write your letter and the closing question in French. Of pages people start on SubhSandesh, 90.9% end up published and shared, so most who begin one finish it.

For a recipient several time zones away, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) can stay locked until a time you set, showing just their name and a countdown before then, and it carries a voice note as long as 60 seconds.

### When a link is the wrong choice

It is not a party invitation, and it does nothing for the children at your own door, who want candy, not a URL. If your recipient is in the same Winnipeg house as you, carve a real pumpkin with them instead.

## Sources

- Adrien Lherm, "Halloween, une vieille fête britannique dans la modernité américaine", *Communications* 77, 2005 (abstract read).
- *Dictionary of Canadianisms on Historical Principles*, DCHP-3, "trick or treat", University of British Columbia, April 2025.
- Environment and Climate Change Canada, Canadian Climate Normals 1981–2010, October values.
- Health Canada, recall of a Halloween witch hat for flammability, updated 11 July 2024.
- National Research Council Canada, "Time zones and daylight saving time", modified 1 November 2025.

Top results: moving2canada.com (two URLs), thecanadianencyclopedia.ca (two URLs, fetch returned empty — judged from snippet), logitgroup.com, a hijacked-subdomain spam page (tashigi.jmoiron.net), universitystudy.ca (now a closure notice), archives.oxfordcounty.ca. Brief framing 'first recorded trick or treat, Alberta 1927' is half right. DCHP-3 (UBC, Apr 2025) dates the chant family to 1917 Ontario ('tricks or treats', Sault Star; 'treat or trick', Owen Sound Sun); 1927 is the first attestation of the exact modern wording, in a report datelined Blackie, Alberta, printed in The Lethbridge Herald (4 Nov per Oxford County archive and others). Barry Popik reports the Calgary Daily Herald ran it on 3 Nov 1927; not opened ourselves, stated in the body as unverified. The Lethbridge 'first' is the newspaper, not the place.

thecanadianencyclopedia.ca, logitgroup.com and archives.oxfordcounty.ca rank top-10 for this keyword, so per BRIEF §4 none is cited; the poll is cited from co-publisher Narrative Research's own release instead (same survey, a URL not in the SERP).

Brief asked for ECCC climate normals 'for 31 Oct'. ECCC normals are monthly; the per-day almanac page is a form that returns nothing to a direct fetch. The post uses October 1981–2010 normals and says so. ECCC's long-term climate extremes API (api.weather.gc.ca ltce-*) gives 31 Oct records (e.g. Edmonton Intl −26.5°C and Yellowknife −27.3°C on 31 Oct 1984) — recorded in the research brief, not used, to stay within 6 outbound links.
Retail Council of Canada: site returned 403 to the fetch; no dated Canadian Halloween spending survey was found, and the post says so instead of printing a figure.
Health Canada: six guessed canada.ca Halloween-safety paths returned 404 and canada.ca site search returned no Halloween page; the safety source is a Health Canada recall (witch hat, flammability).

Not-a-statutory-holiday: verified against the Canada Revenue Agency 2026 public holidays page (no 31 Oct; Thanksgiving 12 Oct to Remembrance Day 11 Nov). It is named in the body but not linked (outbound-link cap of 6). timeanddate.com returned a Cloudflare challenge and was not worked around; weekdays computed locally.
OQLF Grand dictionnaire terminologique (Halloween, n. f.; Quebec 'C'est l'Halloween!') was fetched and verified but not linked: the French-wishes sibling already links it, and the link cap is 6.
Persée: Lherm 2005 full text is page-image scans; only the abstract (bilingual, on the Persée/Érudit record) was read and cited.
Interface of /happy-halloween is English (template-spec); stated in the body for Quebec readers.
